stem: A support assistant budgets prompt size by assuming a fixed number of characters per token, calibrated on English tickets. After launching in Japan and Germany, requests that looked well within budget start exceeding the per-request token limit the team set, and cost forecasts are off. What should the developer do?

options.text: Count tokens on representative samples per language and budget from those counts.
options.why: Token counts per character vary by language and content, so budgets need measured per-language figures from the model's own tokenizer.

options.text: Transliterate all incoming text to ASCII before sending it so that the English ratio applies.
options.why: This destroys meaning in non-Latin scripts and still does not make the ratio accurate.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window so that the budget no longer matters.
options.why: A bigger window does not fix cost forecasts or the team's own per-request budget; the counting method is wrong.

options.text: Lower the character-per-token ratio for every language until the overruns stop appearing in production logs.
options.why: One global ratio still misrepresents each language; the fix guesses instead of measuring.

explanation: Tokens are subword units whose size varies with language and content, so a characters-per-token constant calibrated on English is wrong elsewhere. The token counting endpoint reports what the target model's tokenizer will actually produce, which is the right basis for per-language budgets and forecasts.
reference: Claude API docs — Glossary (tokens); Token counting

stem: A prompt asks Claude to begin every answer with a header line stating the exact word count of the answer that follows. The counts are almost always wrong, even at high effort. What best explains this, and what should the developer do?

options.text: The model counts tokens rather than words; ask for the token count instead.
options.why: The model cannot count its own future output in any unit before generating it.

options.text: Output is generated token by token, so the header is written before the answer exists; count in code.
options.why: Next-token generation means the model must guess a count it has not produced yet; deterministic counting belongs in code.

options.text: Sampling randomness corrupts numbers; request the header again with a lower temperature.
options.why: Randomness is not the cause, and current models reject non-default sampling parameters.

options.text: The model is ignoring the instruction; move it to the system prompt, mark it as critical, and repeat it in the user turn.
options.why: The instruction is being followed; the count is wrong because it is produced before the text exists.

explanation: Claude generates text autoregressively, each token conditioned on what came before. A value that depends on text not yet generated can only be estimated. Put such values at the end, or better, compute them in application code after the response arrives.
reference: Claude API docs — Glossary (tokens); Prompting best practices

stem: A finance team requires that no single request can ever bill more than a fixed number of output tokens. The workload includes hard reasoning cases that need thinking, so quality on those must stay high. A developer proposes setting effort to low to guarantee the cap. Which approach satisfies both requirements?

options.text: Set a thinking budget_tokens value equal to the cap so that the thinking portion of the response can never exceed it.
options.why: Current models reject budget_tokens, and it would not cap the visible answer anyway.

options.text: Set effort to low on every request, since lower effort means fewer output tokens.
options.why: Effort is soft guidance, not a limit, and low effort would hurt the hard cases.

options.text: Keep effort tuned for quality and enforce the cap with max_tokens, handling that stop reason.
options.why: max_tokens is the strict ceiling on thinking plus text; effort shapes how much of it is used.

options.text: Turn thinking off so that output consists only of the visible answer.
options.why: The newest models cannot turn thinking off, and doing so would remove the reasoning the hard cases need.

explanation: Two controls bound cost: effort is soft guidance on how much of the response goes to thinking, while max_tokens is a hard limit on total output for the request. A strict ceiling therefore comes from max_tokens, with code that handles the max_tokens stop reason, while effort stays set for quality.
reference: Claude API docs — Thinking (thinking and effort); Steering thinking (cost control)

stem: An agent runs at high effort with adaptive thinking. Logs show a thinking block on the first request of each turn, but most follow-up requests that only return tool results contain no thinking block at all. A developer concludes thinking is broken on those requests and wants to force it. What should they do?

options.text: Add a system prompt line demanding a thinking block before every tool result is processed, and reject responses without one.
options.why: Prompting cannot mandate a block per request, and it adds tokens without improving outcomes.

options.text: Raise effort to max so that a thinking block is generated on every request, including the tool-result follow-ups.
options.why: No effort level guarantees a thinking block on every request; follow-ups can still skip it.

options.text: Switch to manual extended thinking with a fixed budget for the tool-result requests.
options.why: Current models reject the manual mode, and changing the thinking config would also break the cache.

options.text: Treat it as expected: the model decides per request, and tool-result follow-ups often need no new reasoning.
options.why: With adaptive thinking the first request after user input carries most reasoning; follow-ups that only process results can skip it at any level.

explanation: Adaptive thinking lets the model decide per request whether to think. In a tool-use loop, the first request after new user input typically carries the reasoning, and follow-up requests that only process tool results can skip thinking even at the highest effort. Absence of a block is normal, not a fault.
reference: Claude API docs — Steering thinking (effort levels)

stem: A long-running agent on a current model passes every assistant turn back unchanged. Over a two-hour session, input tokens per request grow much faster than the visible conversation text, and the run eventually nears the context window. The developer suspects the SDK is duplicating messages. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Prior-turn thinking blocks stay in context on current models and are billed as input; clear or compact them when needed.
options.why: On models that keep prior thinking, earlier reasoning remains in the window and is billed as input like any history.

options.text: Cached prefixes are counted twice, once as cache reads and once as input tokens.
options.why: Cache reads and uncached input are separate counters; the total is not double-counted.

options.text: Tool definitions are re-tokenized with each call and the count accumulates across the session.
options.why: Tool definitions cost the same each request; they do not accumulate over time.

options.text: The SDK is resending each assistant message twice on long sessions; deduplicate the messages array in code before every single call.
options.why: The SDK does not duplicate turns; the extra input is legitimate content in the history.

explanation: On current models that preserve thinking across turns, previous thinking blocks remain in the context window and are billed as input tokens like the rest of the conversation. Long agentic sessions therefore accumulate reasoning in context; thinking-block clearing or compaction reclaims space when needed.
reference: Claude API docs — Context windows (the context window with thinking); Thinking

stem: An extraction prompt contains one worked example: an invoice from "Acme Ltd" with all fields filled. In production, when an invoice lacks a field, Claude often fills it with the example's value, and some outputs even name Acme. Which two changes best address this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Wrap the examples in clearly labeled example tags separate from the input document.
options.why: Delimiting examples helps the model distinguish illustration from data to extract.

options.text: Raise effort so the model reasons more carefully before extracting.
options.why: More reasoning does not fix a prompt that demonstrates only one, fully populated case.

options.text: Repeat the same Acme example three times so the format is reinforced.
options.why: Repetition strengthens the exact pattern, including its specific values.

options.text: Lower the temperature so the model sticks closely to the example.
options.why: Sticking more closely to the example is the problem, and current models reject non-default sampling parameters.

options.text: Move the example after the input document so the document is read first.
options.why: Ordering does not teach the missing-field behavior; long inputs belong at the top, examples and query after.

options.text: Add diverse examples, including one where a field is missing and the output shows null for it.
options.why: The model generalizes from examples; showing the missing-field case teaches the right behavior instead of copying.

explanation: A single, fully populated example invites the model to copy its values when the input is ambiguous. Diverse examples that cover edge cases such as missing fields, delimited so they are clearly examples rather than input, correct the pattern. Effort, repetition, and sampling do not address it.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices (use examples effectively)

stem: A marketing tool generates five alternative taglines per request and users complain the five are too similar. The team planned to raise temperature, but the newest model returns a 400 for that parameter. The model must stay the same and cost per request must not rise. What is the best way to get more varied taglines?

options.text: Set top_k instead of temperature, since the two are independent controls.
options.why: Non-default top_k and top_p are rejected on the same models.

options.text: Ask in the prompt for distinct angles, such as tone, audience, and length, with a brief example of each.
options.why: Steering diversity through the prompt works on models that fix sampling parameters.

options.text: Send the same request five times in parallel and take the first tagline from each response, discarding the rest.
options.why: Five calls cost five times as much and may still converge on similar phrasing.

options.text: Lower effort so the model spends less time converging on one style.
options.why: Effort controls how much work goes into the response, not the diversity of its content.

explanation: On the newest models, temperature, top_p, and top_k must stay at their defaults, so diversity has to come from the prompt: explicitly request distinct dimensions of variation and illustrate them. Extra calls multiply cost, and effort is unrelated to variety.
reference: Claude API docs — Thinking (limits and feature compatibility); Prompting best practices

stem: A ticket router must assign one of 40 labels whose boundaries follow house conventions that are not obvious from the label names. Zero-shot with definitions reaches 80% on a labeled set and fails mostly on borderline pairs. The route has a tight latency budget and the prompt prefix is cached. Which two changes best raise accuracy within the budget? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add diverse examples that focus on the confusable label pairs, each in the exact output format.
options.why: Few-shot examples teach conventions that definitions cannot convey, and the borderline pairs are where errors occur.

options.text: Place the examples inside the stable, cached prefix so they add little latency or cost per request.
options.why: A cached prefix makes a longer example set cheap and fast on every call.

options.text: Raise effort to the maximum level so the model deliberates on every ticket.
options.why: Maximum effort adds latency on every request and does not supply the missing conventions.

options.text: Provide exactly one example per label, all written in the same style and length.
options.why: Uniform examples teach surface patterns rather than the boundaries that matter.

options.text: Append the examples to each user message after the cache breakpoint so they stay fresh.
options.why: Content after the breakpoint is billed as uncached input on every request.

options.text: Replace the definitions with longer prose descriptions of each label.
options.why: The failure is in conventions that prose has already failed to convey; examples show them directly.

explanation: When label boundaries follow conventions rather than definitions, few-shot examples are the right tool, and they are most valuable on the confusable cases. Putting the examples in the cached prefix keeps latency and cost flat. Raising effort or lengthening definitions costs more without teaching the boundaries.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices (use examples effectively); Prompt caching

stem:
A document assistant on a model with a large context window returns this for a long session:
```json
{"stop_reason": "model_context_window_exceeded",
 "usage": {"input_tokens": 1200, "cache_read_input_tokens": 996400, "output_tokens": 2100}}
```
The answer is cut off. A teammate proposes raising max_tokens from 8,000 to 32,000. What should the developer do instead?

options.text: Raise max_tokens as proposed, since the model stopped before reaching it.
options.why: The window, not max_tokens, was exhausted; more output room cannot exist.

options.text: Remove the cache breakpoint, because cached tokens are being reported as input and inflating the count against the window.
options.why: Cached tokens still occupy the window; caching changes price, not size.

options.text: Reduce the input, for example by compacting or trimming history, so generation has room in the window.
options.why: Input plus output must fit the window; nearly all of it is already consumed by input.

options.text: Lower effort so the model uses fewer thinking tokens and finishes within the window.
options.why: With only a few thousand tokens of room, no amount of effort tuning makes the answer fit reliably.

explanation: The stop reason says generation hit the model's context window, not the max_tokens cap. Input already fills nearly the whole window, and cached tokens count toward it like any other input. The fix is to shrink the input through compaction, trimming, or splitting the task.
reference: Claude API docs — Context windows (context window overflow behavior); Stop reasons and fallback

stem: A chat feature on a current model with a 40,000-token system prompt has median time to first visible text of 6 seconds and then streams a 300-token answer in 2 seconds. Users judge it slow. The model must not change and eval quality must hold. Which two changes most directly reduce the wait before the first text? (Choose two.)

options.text: Move to a larger model tier for faster reasoning.
options.why: Larger tiers are generally slower, and the model must not change.

options.text: Cache the system prompt so the large prefix is read from cache instead of reprocessed.
options.why: Reading a long prefix from cache reduces time to first token.

options.text: Lower effort one step and confirm on evals that quality holds.
options.why: Less thinking before the answer shortens the pause before text; evals guard quality.

options.text: Enable fast mode on the request.
options.why: Fast mode raises output tokens per second, not time to first token, and the output phase is already short.

options.text: Disable prompt caching so each request is processed on fresh capacity.
options.why: Caching is what shortens prefix processing; removing it makes the wait longer.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the model is not constrained while thinking.
options.why: max_tokens does not affect how long the model takes to start answering.

explanation: The wait before the first text is dominated by prompt processing and thinking. Caching the large prefix cuts processing time, and lowering effort reduces thinking before the answer. Fast mode accelerates the output phase only, and streaming changes delivery rather than time to first token.
reference: Claude API docs — Fast mode (what fast mode does); Prompt caching (pre-warming the cache); Effort

stem: A code assistant runs on an Opus-tier model that supports fast mode. Long answers stream too slowly for paid users, the premium price is approved for the paid tier only, and conversations rely heavily on prompt caching. Product wants the fastest experience for paid users without raising cache misses. Which plan fits every constraint?

options.text: Enable fast mode for all users and recover the cost by lowering effort.
options.why: Premium pricing on free-tier traffic breaks the budget, and lower effort risks quality.

options.text: Keep standard speed and move paid users to a smaller, faster tier instead.
options.why: A smaller tier changes quality; fast mode delivers the same model faster.

options.text: Enable fast mode on any request whose predicted answer is long, regardless of user tier, and keep standard speed otherwise.
options.why: Toggling speed within a conversation invalidates the cache, and it bills premium for free users.

options.text: Set the speed per user for the whole conversation: fast for paid users, standard for the rest.
options.why: Consistent speed within a conversation keeps the cache valid and limits premium spend to the paid tier.

explanation: Fast mode runs the same model with higher output speed at a premium, and switching between fast and standard within a conversation invalidates the prompt cache. Choosing the speed per user for the whole session satisfies the budget, keeps quality, and preserves cache hits.
reference: Claude API docs — Fast mode (considerations); Prompt caching (what invalidates the cache)

stem: An agent turn can involve up to 30 tool calls. To cap spend per turn, a developer sets max_tokens to the whole turn's output budget, yet some turns still bill several times that amount. Quality must not drop on hard turns. What should the developer do first?

options.text: Sum usage across the loop's requests in code and stop or wrap up once the turn budget is reached.
options.why: max_tokens bounds each request, so the turn-level cap must be enforced by the application.

options.text: Lower the number of tools so the model makes fewer calls per turn.
options.why: Fewer tools may change behavior but provides no spend ceiling.

options.text: Divide the turn budget by 30 and use the result as max_tokens on each request so the total can never exceed it.
options.why: This starves hard requests and truncates tool calls while easy ones leave budget unused.

options.text: Set effort to low so total tokens fall below the budget.
options.why: Effort is soft guidance, gives no ceiling, and hurts quality on hard turns.

explanation: In a tool-use loop each request has its own max_tokens, so the parameter cannot bound a whole turn. A per-turn cap belongs in application code: accumulate usage from each response and end the loop, or ask the model to conclude, when the budget is reached.
reference: Claude API docs — Steering thinking (cost control)

stem: A team wants to set the effort level, which the API documents as a request field. In their year-old service, passing the field to the SDK's create method raises an unexpected-argument error, while the same JSON works with curl. What is the most likely cause and the best fix?

options.text: The API rejects the field for their account; ask support to enable it.
options.why: The curl request succeeds, so the API accepts the field.

options.text: The installed SDK predates the field; upgrade it, or pass the field via the SDK's extra-body option meanwhile.
options.why: SDKs are typed wrappers over the REST API and must be updated to know new fields; the escape hatch sends extra params untyped.

options.text: Effort can only be set in the system prompt as an instruction; add it there.
options.why: Effort is an API parameter, not prompt text.

options.text: Replace the SDK with hand-written HTTP calls throughout the service so that new fields never need library support.
options.why: Rewriting the integration loses retries, typed errors, and streaming helpers for a versioning issue.

explanation: The official SDKs wrap the REST API with typed methods. When the API adds a field, an older SDK version does not know it and rejects it client-side even though the API would accept it. Upgrading the SDK is the fix; the SDK's extra-body mechanism bridges the gap without abandoning the library.
reference: Claude API docs — Python SDK (undocumented request params); CLI, SDKs, and libraries

stem: A backend wants to slow its own request rate before it gets rate limited, rather than reacting to 429 errors after the fact. Which signal should the application use?

options.text: The retry-after header, which is present on every successful response.
options.why: retry-after arrives only with a 429, after the limit is already hit.

options.text: The Console usage page, polled by the service every minute.
options.why: The Console is for humans and is not a per-request control signal.

options.text: The rate-limit response headers reporting remaining requests and tokens and when they replenish.
options.why: Every response carries the current limit, remaining capacity, and reset time for proactive throttling.

options.text: A local counter compared against the tier limits published in the documentation, reset at the top of every minute.
options.why: Actual limits vary by organization and workspace and replenish continuously, so a local guess drifts.

explanation: API responses include anthropic-ratelimit headers with the enforced limit, remaining capacity, and reset time. Reading them lets the application throttle before hitting a 429, whereas retry-after only appears once a limit has been exceeded.
reference: Claude API docs — Rate limits (response headers)

stem: At month end every request from a service starts failing with HTTP 429 and error type rate_limit_error. The SDK's automatic retries and the service's own backoff loop keep retrying for hours, and the on-call engineer sees no retry-after header on the responses. What is the best response?

options.text: Route traffic to a different model, since rate limits are applied per model.
options.why: A spend cap applies to the organization, not one model's rate limit.

options.text: Rotate the API key, because the old key's quota is exhausted.
options.why: Spend caps are organizational; a new key shares the same cap.

options.text: Increase the backoff ceiling and jitter so retries spread out over several hours until capacity returns on its own.
options.why: This is not a transient capacity problem; retries will fail until access is restored.

options.text: Check the error details for the spend-limit code, stop retrying, and alert to raise the limit or await the reset.
options.why: A 429 without retry-after that carries the spend-limit code means the monthly cap was reached; retrying cannot succeed.

explanation: A tier spend cap returns 429 rate_limit_error like a rate limit, but with no retry-after header and a spend-limit error code in the details. Because it persists until the cap is raised or the month resets, the correct handling is to recognize it, stop retrying, and escalate rather than turn a billing event into a retry storm.
reference: Claude API docs — Rate limits (reaching your spend cap); Claude API errors

stem: A Python endpoint must classify 150 short records per user request and return within a few seconds. It currently calls the API for each record one after another with the synchronous client, taking over a minute. Rate limits are moderate. Which change best fits?

options.text: Use the async client and issue the calls concurrently with a bounded concurrency limit.
options.why: Concurrent requests cut wall-clock time, and the bound keeps the service inside its rate limits.

options.text: Start 150 threads at once so every record is processed in parallel.
options.why: Unbounded parallelism invites 429s and retries, and adds no benefit over a bounded pool.

options.text: Enable streaming for each call so results begin arriving sooner.
options.why: Streaming does not shorten sequential calls; the total time is unchanged.

options.text: Submit the 150 records as a single Message Batch and return the classifications to the user when the batch completes.
options.why: Batches are asynchronous with long completion windows, unsuitable for a request that must return in seconds.

explanation: Sequential calls make latency the sum of all requests. The SDK's async client lets the service run many requests concurrently, and a concurrency limit keeps the burst within rate limits. Batching is for offline work, and streaming does not parallelize anything.
reference: Claude API docs — Python SDK (async usage); Rate limits

stem: A backend streams responses from the API and relays them to browsers. In production, users see nothing for the whole generation and then the full answer appears at once, while the same code streams token by token on a developer laptop. Production sits behind a company API gateway. What should the developer fix first?

options.text: Switch the browser connection to a WebSocket opened directly to the Claude API so the gateway is no longer in the path.
options.why: The Messages API streams over server-sent events, and exposing it to browsers would leak the key.

options.text: Configure the gateway to pass server-sent events through unbuffered, flushing each event to the client.
options.why: A buffering proxy holds the streamed events until the response ends, which matches the symptom.

options.text: Replace streaming with a non-streaming call, since the gateway cannot handle long responses.
options.why: This gives up incremental delivery and reintroduces long-request timeout risk.

options.text: Increase the SDK request timeout so that the stream is not cut short.
options.why: The stream completes; the symptom is delayed delivery, not a timeout.

explanation: When streaming works locally but arrives all at once in production, an intermediary that buffers the response is the usual cause. Server-sent events must be forwarded as they arrive; the fix is at the gateway, not in the SDK or the API protocol.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages

stem: One service exposes an interactive autocomplete route that must fail fast within two seconds and a report route that legitimately runs for several minutes. Both use the same SDK client with default timeout and retries. How should the developer configure this?

options.text: Set the client timeout to two seconds so that no request can hang.
options.why: The report route would time out and be retried, never completing.

options.text: Set the client timeout to ten minutes and rely on the interactive route's own UI spinner.
options.why: Autocomplete could hang for minutes, missing its two-second requirement.

options.text: Share one client and override timeout and retries per request for each route.
options.why: The SDK allows per-request options, so each route gets its own budget without a second client.

options.text: Construct a fresh client with the right timeout inside every request handler.
options.why: Building a client per request wastes connections and setup; per-request options exist for this.

explanation: SDK clients accept defaults for timeout and retries and let you override them per request. One shared client with per-route overrides gives the autocomplete route a short timeout and few retries, and the report route (ideally streamed) a long one, without connection churn.
reference: Claude API docs — Python SDK (timeouts; retries)

stem: A mobile app streams long answers through the team's backend. On flaky networks the client connection drops mid-answer; users reconnect within seconds and expect the same answer to continue rather than start over. Cost must not double. Which two design choices best meet this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use non-streaming calls so there is no partial state to manage.
options.why: Long non-streaming requests risk timeouts and give the user nothing until the end.

options.text: Have the client call the Claude API directly so the backend is not in the path.
options.why: This exposes the API key and still loses the stream on disconnect.

options.text: Lower max_tokens so answers finish before connections drop.
options.why: Truncating answers does not address reconnection and harms quality.

options.text: Have the backend buffer each answer's deltas under a job ID so a reconnecting client resumes from its last offset.
options.why: A server-side buffer decouples the API stream from the fragile client connection.

options.text: Keep the upstream API stream running for a short grace period after a client disconnect instead of aborting immediately.
options.why: Continuing lets the same answer finish for a client that returns within seconds.

options.text: On reconnect, resend the original request to the API and stream the new answer.
options.why: This bills the request again and, because outputs vary, the user sees a different answer.

explanation: Resumable delivery requires separating the API stream from the client connection: the backend consumes the stream into a per-job buffer and lets the client resume by offset. Re-issuing the request would double cost and, given non-determinism, produce a different answer.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages (error recovery)

stem: An interactive app prefers fast mode on an Opus-tier model but has a strict latency budget. During peaks, fast-mode requests return 429 with a retry-after of several seconds, and the SDK's default retries wait and retry at fast speed, blowing the budget. Transient errors such as overloads must still be retried. Which approach fits all of this?

options.text: Fire fast and standard requests together for every call and use whichever response finishes first, cancelling the other one.
options.why: Every request is billed twice, and the standard one usually wins anyway during peaks.

options.text: Keep defaults and raise the client timeout so retries have time to succeed.
options.why: A longer timeout makes the latency budget worse, not better.

options.text: Set max_retries to zero on the client so no request ever waits on retry-after.
options.why: This also disables retries for overloads and server errors, which the requirement forbids.

options.text: Send the fast request with zero retries, catch the rate-limit error, and reissue at standard speed with default retries.
options.why: Failing fast on the fast-mode limit and falling back keeps latency bounded while transient errors are still retried.

explanation: Fast mode has its own rate limit. To fall back rather than wait, disable automatic retries on the fast attempt only, catch the rate-limit error, and reissue the request at standard speed with normal retries so that overloads and server errors are still handled.
reference: Claude API docs — Fast mode (retries and fallback)

stem: A research agent runs for up to ten minutes per task. Users start tasks from a mobile app that is often backgrounded, may check progress from a second device, and the backend pods restart during deploys. Progress must survive all of this without repeating the task. Which architecture best fits?

options.text: Run the task in a worker that appends events to a durable job log; clients fetch or subscribe by job ID from any device.
options.why: Durable per-job state survives disconnects and restarts and is readable from anywhere.

options.text: Make one non-streaming API call per task and have the app poll for the final result.
options.why: The call still dies with the pod, and users get no progress for minutes.

options.text: Have the phone hold a streaming connection to the backend and reconnect and restart the task if it drops.
options.why: Restarting repeats the work and cost every time the app is backgrounded.

options.text: Open a WebSocket from the handling pod to the phone and stream the agent's events over it for the whole run, reconnecting on drops.
options.why: The run dies with the pod or the backgrounded app, and a second device has no connection.

explanation: When clients are intermittent and servers restart, the unit of durability must be the job, not the connection. A worker consumes the API stream and records events durably; clients read progress by job ID through polling or a subscription, from any device, without re-running the task.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages; Claude API errors (long requests)

stem:
A service is throttled with 429 errors naming the input-tokens-per-minute limit during peaks. A typical response shows:
```json
{"usage": {"input_tokens": 31200, "cache_creation_input_tokens": 0,
           "cache_read_input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 400}}
```
About 30,000 of those tokens are an identical instruction set on every request. The prompt cannot be shortened and the fix must ship today. What should the developer do?

options.text: Move peak traffic to the Message Batches API, which has separate rate limits, and return results when the batch completes.
options.why: Batches are asynchronous with long completion windows, unsuitable for live requests.

options.text: Cache the shared instruction prefix, since cache reads do not count toward the input-token limit on most models.
options.why: Turning 30,000 uncached tokens per request into cache reads removes most of the counted input.

options.text: Request a higher rate limit and keep the current request shape until it is granted.
options.why: A limit increase takes time and does not ship today.

options.text: Add exponential backoff so peak requests are retried until capacity frees up.
options.why: Backoff smooths bursts but does not raise throughput; the limit is still hit.

explanation: Uncached input and cache writes count toward the input-tokens-per-minute limit, but cache reads do not on most models. The usage shows the shared prefix is processed uncached every time. Caching it multiplies effective throughput immediately, which neither backoff nor a pending limit increase does.
reference: Claude API docs — Rate limits (cache-aware ITPM); Prompt caching

stem: A worker pulls jobs from a queue, calls Claude, then emails the result to the customer and marks the job done. After a crash between the API call and the database update, the restarted worker re-ran the job, billed the call again, and sent a second, differently worded email. What should the developer change?

options.text: Send the email before calling the API so the customer is notified even if the call fails.
options.why: This sends an email with no content and does nothing about re-runs.

options.text: Deduplicate by hashing the response text and skipping the email whenever the same hash has already been sent for that customer.
options.why: Responses vary between runs, so the hashes differ and the duplicate is not caught.

options.text: Record the result under the job ID before any side effect, and on restart check that record before calling or emailing.
options.why: Recording state at each step makes the job idempotent regardless of when the crash happens.

options.text: Set the SDK's max_retries to zero so the API call is never repeated.
options.why: The repeat came from the worker re-running the job, not from SDK retries.

explanation: Model outputs are non-deterministic, so duplicate work cannot be detected by comparing responses. Idempotency must come from state: store the result under the job ID before side effects, and make each step check that state on restart so a crash never repeats the call or the email.
reference: Claude API docs — Glossary (temperature; non-determinism); Python SDK (retries)

stem: In a shared whiteboard app, one user asks Claude a question and all 20 participants in the room should watch the same answer appear live. The current build has each participant's client request the answer through the backend, so 20 API calls run and participants see slightly different text. Cost and consistency both matter. Which design fixes this?

options.text: Have the first participant's client forward the finished answer to the others when it completes.
options.why: Participants would wait for the whole answer and depend on one client's connection.

options.text: Keep the 20 calls but set temperature to zero on each of them so that every participant receives exactly the same text.
options.why: Non-default temperature is rejected on current models, and even at zero, outputs are not guaranteed identical.

options.text: Keep 20 calls and cache the prompt so the repeated requests are almost free.
options.why: Caching cuts input cost only; 20 outputs are still billed and still differ.

options.text: Make one API call for the room and broadcast its stream deltas to every participant over the room connection.
options.why: A single generation is billed once and every viewer sees the same text as it arrives.

explanation: Because generation is non-deterministic and billed per call, fan-out must happen after the model: generate once on the server and broadcast the streamed deltas to every participant. Sampling settings cannot make separate calls identical, and caching does not remove output cost.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages; Glossary (temperature)

stem: A team's deep-research agent runs for hours across many sources. On an Opus-tier model at the highest effort with a large max_tokens, evals still miss the accuracy bar on multistep synthesis. Budget is not the constraint. What should the team try next?

options.text: Evaluate the Fable tier, the documented next step when Opus at its highest effort levels still falls short.
options.why: The Fable tier sits above Opus for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work.

options.text: Split the work across several Sonnet-tier subagents so that more sources are covered in parallel within the same time.
options.why: More coverage does not fix synthesis accuracy that the more capable tier is built for.

options.text: Add a fixed thinking budget on top of the effort setting to force deeper reasoning.
options.why: Current Opus models reject budget_tokens; effort is already at its highest level.

options.text: Enable fast mode on the Opus-tier model to give it more throughput per hour.
options.why: Fast mode changes speed, not capability.

explanation: The current lineup places the Fable tier above Opus: the documentation recommends starting with Opus for most workloads and moving to Fable when evals at the highest effort levels still fall short on demanding reasoning or long-horizon agentic work.
reference: Claude API docs — Choosing the right model; Models overview

stem: A team has chosen an Opus-tier model because its product needs fast mode and 1-hour prompt caching. Compliance requires running through a specific cloud platform rather than the Claude API directly. What should the developer do first?

options.text: Assume feature parity, since the same model is served on every platform.
options.why: Feature availability differs by platform even for the same model.

options.text: Check the platform's documented feature support for that model before committing to the design.
options.why: Each platform's page lists which features it supports; the design should rest on that.

options.text: Build on the Claude API now to hit the deadline and plan to move to the required platform after launch.
options.why: Moving later risks discovering unsupported features after users depend on them.

options.text: Pick a Haiku-tier model instead, since smaller models are supported everywhere.
options.why: Tier does not determine platform feature support, and it changes the product's quality.

explanation: The same model can be offered with different feature support on different platforms. Before committing to features such as fast mode or extended cache durations, verify them against the platform's documented support matrix rather than assuming parity or deferring the check.
reference: Claude API docs — Fast mode (considerations); Prompt caching (1-hour cache duration)

stem: An extraction pipeline guarantees JSON by forcing its single extraction tool with tool_choice of type tool. After moving to the newest model, every request fails with a 400 that names tool_choice. Output must remain schema-valid. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Change tool_choice to type any so the model must call some tool while still choosing which one to use.
options.why: Forced tool use of either kind is rejected on these models.

options.text: Turn thinking off, since forced tool use conflicts with thinking.
options.why: Thinking cannot be turned off on these models; the request would still fail.

options.text: Use automatic tool choice with strict tool use, or structured outputs, and validate the result.
options.why: These give schema-valid output on the newest models without forcing a call.

options.text: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace to force JSON.
options.why: Prefill is not supported on current models and returns a 400.

explanation: The newest models reject forced tool choice because it would skip always-on thinking. Schema guarantees now come from strict tool use with automatic tool choice or from structured outputs, followed by validation in code. Disabling thinking and prefill are also rejected on these models.
reference: Claude API docs — What's new in Claude Fable 5.1 (breaking changes); Thinking (thinking with tool use)

stem: A service never sets effort. After switching to a newer Opus-tier model, cost per request fell noticeably and eval scores on the hardest cases dipped, while easy cases were unchanged. Nothing else in the request changed. What best explains this and what should the team do?

options.text: The newer tokenizer produces fewer tokens, which lowers both cost and reasoning depth.
options.why: Tokenizer changes affect token counts and cost, not reasoning depth on hard cases.

options.text: The new model ignores the system prompt more often; move the key instructions into the user turn and repeat them each request.
options.why: Nothing suggests instruction loss; easy cases are unchanged.

options.text: The newer model is weaker on hard reasoning; roll back to the previous model.
options.why: Rolling back discards the upgrade without testing the obvious variable.

options.text: The default effort differs between releases; set effort explicitly and re-run an effort sweep on the evals.
options.why: An unset effort inherits each model's default, which changed; explicit values restore control.

explanation: Effort defaults are set per model, and a release can change the default. A request that omits effort therefore runs at whatever the new model defaults to, which explains lower cost and lower depth on hard cases. Set effort explicitly and choose the level from an eval sweep rather than carrying assumptions across releases.
reference: Claude API docs — Effort (recommended effort levels; best practices)

stem: A production assistant pins a model ID. A newer model in the same tier is available, and the team wants to adopt it with a way to attribute any regression and roll back quickly. Which two practices best support that? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run the new model on a sample of real traffic in shadow mode and compare eval metrics against the current model.
options.why: Shadow evaluation surfaces regressions on real inputs before users are affected.

options.text: Roll out by percentage with the model ID recorded per request, keeping the old ID configured for immediate rollback.
options.why: Attributable, reversible rollout isolates the model change as the variable.

options.text: Point the service at the tier's dateless ID so future releases apply automatically.
options.why: Dateless IDs on current generations are pinned snapshots, and automatic changes defeat attribution.

options.text: Compare the two models by checking that outputs match the stored responses exactly.
options.why: Outputs vary run to run even on one model; exact-match comparison is meaningless.

options.text: Switch all traffic on the old model's retirement date to minimize the number of changes.
options.why: A single cutover at the deadline leaves no time to attribute or fix regressions.

options.text: Skip evals because models within one tier behave the same.
options.why: Releases change behavior even within a tier; evals are the safeguard.

explanation: Adopting a new model safely means treating it as a controlled change: measure it on real inputs before exposure, then roll out gradually with the model recorded per request and the old model ready for rollback. Automatic version drift and exact-match comparisons undermine both attribution and reliability.
reference: Claude API docs — Model IDs and versioning; Choosing the right model (decide whether to upgrade)

stem: After moving a coding agent to a newer model, task success is unchanged but cost and wall-clock time rose: traces show the model reading files one per turn where it used to batch several reads, and rewriting whole files for small edits. Which two actions should the team take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add prompt guidance from the model's prompting guide to batch independent tool calls and prefer targeted edits.
options.why: These are documented behavior differences with prompt-level fixes.

options.text: Re-run the eval suite with cost and turn-count metrics to confirm the prompt change fixes it.
options.why: Behavior changes must be measured, not assumed fixed.

options.text: Roll back to the previous model until the new one is patched.
options.why: Model IDs are fixed snapshots; the behavior will not change, and the fix is in the prompt.

options.text: Raise effort so the model plans more calls per turn.
options.why: Higher effort tends to add tokens and calls rather than batch them.

options.text: Enable fast mode to offset the extra turns with faster output.
options.why: Fast mode does not reduce turns or tokens and adds premium cost.

options.text: Reduce max_tokens so whole-file rewrites are cut short.
options.why: Truncated rewrites produce broken files.

explanation: Model releases can change agentic habits such as how many tool calls run per turn or how edits are made, without changing success rates. The documented remedy is prompting guidance specific to the new model, verified with evals that track cost and turns, rather than reverting or adding tokens.
reference: Claude API docs — What's new in Claude Fable 5.1 (behavior differences); Effort (effort with tool use)

stem:
A contract-review feature must pass at least 95% of the eval set, answer with p95 latency of 5 seconds or less, and cost no more than 2.5 times the cheapest option per request. The team measured:
```
Haiku tier            84% pass   p95 1.4 s   cost 1.0x
Sonnet tier, low      91% pass   p95 2.1 s   cost 1.6x
Sonnet tier, high     96% pass   p95 4.2 s   cost 2.3x
Opus tier, medium     97% pass   p95 6.8 s   cost 4.0x
```
Which configuration should ship?

options.text: Sonnet tier at high effort, the only option meeting quality, latency, and cost.
options.why: 96% passes, 4.2 s is under 5 s, and 2.3x is within 2.5x.

options.text: Opus tier at medium effort, because it has the highest pass rate and the extra cost is justified by quality.
options.why: It violates both the latency and the cost constraints.

options.text: Haiku tier, because it is fastest and cheapest.
options.why: It misses the 95% quality bar.

options.text: Sonnet tier at low effort, the best balance of speed and cost.
options.why: It also misses the quality bar.

explanation: Model selection is a constraint problem: every stated bar must be met, not just the one that looks most important. Only Sonnet at high effort satisfies the quality floor, the latency ceiling, and the cost ceiling at once; the others fail at least one.
reference: Claude API docs — Choosing the right model (establish key criteria); Effort

stem: A legacy pipeline built for an older model generation uses extended thinking with budget_tokens, temperature 0, an assistant prefill of an opening brace to force JSON, and a pinned dated model ID. It must move to the newest tier with no request failures. Which three changes are required? (Choose three.)

options.text: Use an alias instead of a pinned ID so future upgrades are automatic.
options.why: Current model IDs are pinned snapshots, and automatic upgrades are not what a controlled migration wants.

options.text: Replace the budget_tokens thinking configuration with adaptive thinking steered by effort.
options.why: Manual extended thinking with budget_tokens is rejected on current models.

options.text: Remove the temperature setting and get consistency from the prompt and validation.
options.why: Non-default sampling parameters return a 400 on the newest models.

options.text: Replace the prefill with structured outputs or strict tool use plus validation.
options.why: Prefilling the assistant turn is not supported on current models.

options.text: Add a beta header to unlock the larger context window.
options.why: The large context window is the default on current models; no header is needed.

options.text: Switch to forced tool choice to guarantee the JSON shape.
options.why: Forced tool choice is rejected on the newest models.

explanation: Migrating across generations means removing every parameter the target model rejects: manual thinking budgets, non-default sampling, and assistant prefill. The replacements are effort-steered adaptive thinking, prompt-based consistency, and structured outputs or strict tools. Forced tool choice would introduce a new failure, and the large context needs no header.
reference: Claude API docs — Claude API errors (common validation errors); Migration guides

stem: A data-cleanup task is retried automatically up to three attempts; if all fail, a human fixes it at a cost of 2.00 per task. Measured per-attempt cost and first-attempt success rates are: Haiku tier 0.010 and 60%, Sonnet tier 0.030 and 92%, Opus tier 0.150 and 98%. Quality after success is equivalent. Which tier minimizes expected cost per completed task?

options.text: Haiku tier, because its per-attempt cost is lowest by far.
options.why: With 40% failures, retries and frequent human fixes make its expected cost about 0.14 per task.

options.text: Sonnet tier, because its expected retries and human fixes stay small relative to its attempt cost.
options.why: Roughly 1.09 attempts at 0.030 plus a negligible human-fix share gives about 0.034 per task.

options.text: Opus tier, because the highest success rate means the fewest attempts and almost never any human fixes to pay for.
options.why: Its attempt cost dominates at about 0.15 per task, several times the Sonnet figure.

options.text: It cannot be determined without token counts for each tier.
options.why: Per-attempt cost already reflects tokens; the expected-value calculation needs nothing more.

explanation: Cost per completed task combines expected attempts and the cost of eventual failure. Haiku: about 1.56 attempts (0.016) plus a 6.4% chance of a 2.00 human fix (0.128), about 0.144. Sonnet: about 1.09 attempts (0.033) plus a 0.05% human-fix chance, about 0.034. Opus: about 1.02 attempts, about 0.153. The cheapest attempt is not the cheapest completion.
reference: Claude API docs — Choosing the right model (decide whether to upgrade or change models)

stem: To save money, a router sends hard turns to the most capable tier and routine turns to an Opus-tier model within the same conversation, passing every assistant turn back unchanged. Users report that after a routine turn the assistant seems to forget the reasoning it did on the previous hard turn, though no request fails. What is the best fix?

options.text: Ask the capable model to write its reasoning into the visible text so the reasoning survives the switch to the other model.
options.why: This leaks internal reasoning to users and bloats every response to work around routing.

options.text: Strip thinking blocks before each switch so both models see a clean history.
options.why: The reasoning is already lost on the switch; removing it everywhere makes continuity worse.

options.text: Choose the model per conversation rather than per turn, so reasoning stays readable across the session.
options.why: Thinking blocks are readable only by the model that produced them and certain others; a downward switch silently drops them.

options.text: Raise effort on the Opus-tier model so it reconstructs the earlier reasoning.
options.why: More effort cannot recover reasoning the model never received.

explanation: Thinking blocks are bound to the model that produced them; a less capable model cannot read a more capable model's blocks, and the API drops them without error. Per-turn routing between tiers therefore loses reasoning on every downward switch. Route per conversation, or escalate only upward, and evaluate the cost tradeoff on real sessions.
reference: Claude API docs — Thinking (switching models mid-conversation); What's new in Claude Fable 5.1

stem: A team's cost dashboard reads usage from the message_start event of each streamed response. Input tokens look right, but output tokens are recorded as one or two per request even for long answers. What should the developer change?

options.text: Make a second non-streaming call with the same prompt after the stream ends to obtain the accurate usage figures.
options.why: This doubles cost and the second answer's usage differs anyway.

options.text: Call the token counting endpoint on the assembled answer text.
options.why: Token counting is for inputs and would miss thinking tokens billed as output.

options.text: Count the characters in the streamed text and divide by an average token length.
options.why: Estimates drift from billed counts; the API reports the exact figure.

options.text: Take the final cumulative usage from message_delta, or from the SDK's accumulated final message.
options.why: The usage on message_delta is cumulative and reflects the completed response.

explanation: In a stream, message_start carries the input-side usage and only a placeholder output count. The message_delta events carry cumulative usage, so the final one holds the billed output tokens; SDK helpers that accumulate the final message expose the same figures.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages (event types)

stem: A support assistant has a 50,000-token cached system prompt. After each deploy, and after quiet periods, the first user request is noticeably slower because the cache entry has to be written. The team wants first users to get cached latency too. Which technique fits?

options.text: Send a pre-warm request with max_tokens of zero using the same prefix and settings after deploy and on a schedule.
options.why: A zero-output request writes the cache without generating anything, so real users hit it.

options.text: Enable automatic caching so the entry is created before the first request.
options.why: Automatic caching only chooses the breakpoint; an entry still requires a request.

options.text: Reduce the system prompt below the minimum cacheable length so it needs no cache.
options.why: The prompt would still be processed on every request, now at full price.

options.text: Switch the breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so the entry survives quiet periods and deploys without any extra requests.
options.why: A longer TTL helps within an hour, but nothing creates the entry after a deploy until some request writes it.

explanation: Cache entries are written by requests. A pre-warm request with max_tokens of zero reads the prompt into the model, writes the cache at the breakpoint, and returns without output, so the first real user gets a cache hit. It must use the same prefix, thinking, and effort settings as the real requests.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (pre-warming the cache)

stem: An agent step on a large shared prefix takes about four minutes to generate, and the next step is sent about ninety seconds after the previous one finishes. The prefix uses the default cache TTL, yet nearly every step shows a cache write and no read. What is the cause and the fix?

options.text: The breakpoint is on a changing block; move it to the last stable block.
options.why: The prefix is identical between steps; timing, not placement, is the problem.

options.text: The lifetime runs from the start of the request, so generation time consumes it; use the 1-hour TTL for this prefix.
options.why: Four minutes of generation plus ninety seconds exceeds five minutes from request start.

options.text: Long responses are never cached; add a second breakpoint after the assistant turn so the next step can find an entry.
options.why: Response length does not disable caching, and another breakpoint does not extend the lifetime.

options.text: Cache writes are expected on every step because each step adds new blocks.
options.why: New blocks are written, but the stable prefix should still be read if the entry were alive.

explanation: The cache lifetime starts when the writing or reading request begins, not when its response ends. A step that generates for four minutes leaves only about a minute for the next request to arrive under the default TTL. When generation time eats the window, the 1-hour TTL is the right tool.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (how prompt caching works; 1-hour cache duration)

stem: An assistant has a large, stable system prompt and tool set, followed by a conversation that grows with each turn. Users often pause for twenty minutes between turns, but within an active exchange turns arrive every minute. The team wants to combine cache TTLs. Which two rules should their design follow? (Choose two.)

options.text: Put a 1-hour breakpoint at the end of the stable prefix and a default 5-minute breakpoint on the conversation tail.
options.why: The prefix survives pauses at a higher write price once, while the cheap tail refreshes during active exchanges.

options.text: Ensure every 1-hour breakpoint appears before any 5-minute breakpoint in the request.
options.why: Longer-TTL entries must precede shorter ones; the API rejects the reverse order.

options.text: Use the 1-hour TTL on every breakpoint so nothing expires during a pause.
options.why: Writing the growing tail at double price on every turn wastes the savings.

options.text: Use only 5-minute breakpoints and rely on automatic refresh to bridge the pauses.
options.why: Refresh happens only when a request arrives; a twenty-minute pause outlives the entry.

options.text: Put the 5-minute breakpoint on the system prompt and the 1-hour breakpoint on the latest user message.
options.why: This reverses the required order and caches the volatile tail for an hour.

options.text: Set a 1-hour TTL on the tool definitions and a 5-minute TTL on the system prompt to keep costs down.
options.why: The system prompt is stable and would then expire during pauses despite its size.

explanation: Mixed TTLs let a stable prefix be written once at the 1-hour price while the growing conversation uses the cheaper 5-minute entries that refresh for free during active use. The constraint is ordering: 1-hour breakpoints must come before 5-minute ones in the request.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (mixing different TTLs; when to use the 1-hour cache)

stem: An internal tool sends a stable 20,000-token instruction prefix on every request, but it receives only about six requests per hour, spread roughly ten minutes apart. After the developer added a cache breakpoint with the default lifetime, the input cost for the tool went up by about a quarter instead of down. What should the developer do?

options.text: Give the breakpoint the 1-hour lifetime so one write per hour serves the remaining requests as reads.
options.why: Requests ten minutes apart fall within an hour, so a single higher-priced write is followed by cheap reads instead of a fresh write each time.

options.text: Remove the breakpoint, since caching only pays off for high-volume traffic.
options.why: The prefix is reused within the hour; the longer lifetime turns it into a saving rather than a loss.

options.text: Split the prefix across several breakpoints so each request writes a smaller entry.
options.why: Every entry still expires before the next request, so each request still pays the write price for the whole prefix.

options.text: Send a pre-warm request with max_tokens of zero immediately before each real request.
options.why: That adds a write before every request and then a read, costing more than the current setup.

explanation: A cache write costs more than uncached input, and a read costs much less. With the default lifetime, an entry written by one request has expired by the time the next one arrives ten minutes later, so every request pays the write premium and never reads. The 1-hour lifetime costs more for the single write but keeps the entry alive across the hour, so the other requests read it at the discounted rate.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (1-hour cache duration; when to use the 1-hour cache; pricing)

stem: A prompt consists of a large tool set that changes only with releases, a product-catalog block regenerated every morning, and a set of examples updated weekly, followed by the user turn. A single cache breakpoint sits at the end of the examples. Each morning's catalog change causes a full-price rewrite of everything. How should the breakpoints be arranged?

options.text: Reorder the prompt so the catalog comes first, because the most volatile content should be cached first and refreshed daily.
options.why: Stable content belongs first; volatile content early invalidates everything after it.

options.text: Regenerate the catalog less often so that rewrites happen weekly instead of daily.
options.why: This changes the product's freshness to work around a cache layout problem.

options.text: Move the single breakpoint to the end of the tool set so the tools are always cached.
options.why: The catalog and examples would then be uncached input on every request.

options.text: Put breakpoints after the tools, after the catalog, and after the examples, so a change rewrites only what follows.
options.why: Sections that change at different frequencies get their own entries; the daily change no longer rewrites the tools.

explanation: Cache entries cover the prefix up to each breakpoint, and a change invalidates everything after it. Placing breakpoints at the boundaries between sections with different change rates means a daily catalog update rewrites the catalog and what follows, while the large tool set stays a cache read. Up to four breakpoints are available.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (when to use multiple breakpoints; what invalidates the cache)

stem:
A request on a model whose cache reads are billed at 0.1 times base input returns:
```json
{"usage": {"input_tokens": 1200, "cache_creation_input_tokens": 0,
           "cache_read_input_tokens": 48000, "output_tokens": 900}}
```
With I as the base input price per token and O as the output price per token, what is the request's cost?

options.why: 1,200 uncached at I, plus 48,000 cache reads at 0.1 × I (4,800 × I), plus output.
This applies the cache-write multiplier to tokens that were read, not written.
This bills the cached tokens at full input price.
This ignores the cache reads entirely.

explanation: Each usage counter is billed at its own rate: uncached input at base price, cache writes at the write multiplier, cache reads at the read multiplier for that model, and output at the output price. Here the 48,000 cached tokens cost 4,800 × I, so total input cost is 6,000 × I plus 900 × O for output.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (pricing; tracking cache performance)

stem: A pipeline fans out 50 parallel requests that share a new 100,000-token document prefix with a cache breakpoint. Usage on all 50 shows cache_creation_input_tokens near 100,000 and cache_read_input_tokens of 0, so the run costs far more than modeled. Subsequent runs on the same document hit the cache fine. What should the developer change?

options.text: Switch the breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so the entry exists before the fan-out.
options.why: TTL controls how long an entry lives, not when it becomes available.

options.text: Send one request first and start the other 49 once its response begins, so they read the entry it wrote.
options.why: A cache entry becomes available only after the first response begins; parallel requests that start before then all write.

options.text: Add a second breakpoint earlier in the document so half of the prefix is cached.
options.why: Every request would still start before any entry exists at either breakpoint.

options.text: Use the Message Batches API instead, which guarantees cache hits across all requests submitted in the same batch.
options.why: Batch cache hits are best effort, and batches add hours of latency.

explanation: A cache entry only becomes available once the first response that writes it begins. Fifty simultaneous requests on a brand-new prefix each pay the write. Sending one request first, or pre-warming, and then fanning out lets the rest read the entry, which is why later runs already hit.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (cache limitations; pre-warming the cache)

stem: A Go service sends the same 12 tools on every request and the tool list in source never changes, yet only about half of requests report cache reads. Requests arrive a few seconds apart, and every missed request shows cache_creation_input_tokens equal to the full tools-plus-system prefix, while every hit shows the full prefix as cache_read_input_tokens. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: The 5-minute lifetime is expiring between requests; switch to the 1-hour lifetime.
options.why: Requests a few seconds apart cannot outlive the default lifetime.

options.text: The tool definitions exceed the cacheable limit; describe some tools in the system prompt instead.
options.why: There is no such limit, and the hits show the full prefix is cacheable; tools described in prose cannot be called.

options.text: Tool schemas are serialized with nondeterministic key order, so the bytes differ; serialize in a stable order.
options.why: Go randomizes map iteration order, so identical tools can serialize differently and the cache sees a changed prefix.

options.text: The tools breakpoint is missing; add cache_control to the last tool.
options.why: With no breakpoint there would be no full-prefix reads at all, yet half of the requests hit.

explanation: Cache hits require a byte-identical prefix. Some languages, Go among them, randomize map key order during JSON serialization, so the same tool schema can be emitted differently from one request to the next; the cache sees changed tools and writes a new entry. Expiry and a missing breakpoint are ruled out by the timing and by the requests that do hit. The fix is deterministic serialization with stable key and tool order.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (troubleshooting; what invalidates the cache)

stem: Analysts upload 300-page contracts and then ask 20 or more questions per document over a few hours. Answers must reason across distant sections of the same document, and the token budget is tight. The current build resends the full contract uncached with each question. Which two changes best fit? (Choose two.)

options.text: Count the document's tokens on upload to confirm it fits with room for history and to estimate the session's cost.
options.why: Budgeting starts from the real token count for the target model.

options.text: Chunk the contract and retrieve only the passages that match each question.
options.why: Retrieval risks missing the cross-section dependencies the answers require.

options.text: Queue the questions and answer them overnight through the Message Batches API.
options.why: Analysts ask interactively; hours of latency does not fit.

options.text: Summarize the contract once and answer every question from the summary.
options.why: A summary drops the clause-level detail contract questions depend on.

options.text: Put the question before the contract so the model reads it first.
options.why: Long documents belong at the top with the query after them, and a leading question breaks the shared prefix.

options.text: Send the contract as the stable prefix with a 1-hour cache breakpoint and place each question after it.
options.why: Questions spread over hours read the document at the cache rate instead of re-billing it every time.

explanation: When many questions target one large document within hours, the document is the cacheable prefix: a 1-hour breakpoint lets each question read it cheaply while retaining full cross-section context. Counting tokens up front confirms the fit and grounds the cost model. Chunking and summarizing trade away the reasoning the task needs.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt caching (when to use the 1-hour cache); Token counting; Prompting best practices (long context)
